Memory Jogger.new: In the Court's first major constitutional decision, a South Carolina executor sued Georgia on a Revolutionary War debt; the Justices held 4--1, in seriatim opinions, that Article III lets a citizen of one State sue another State without its consent---a ruling the Eleventh Amendment promptly overturned (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/2/419/}{Justia}).

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court, exercising original jurisdiction, ruled for the plaintiff by a \textbf{4--1} vote and ordered that default judgment be entered unless Georgia appeared or showed cause. The case was argued on February 5, 1793, and decided on February 19, 1793 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/2/419/}{Justia}):
Five Justices participated, and the seriatim opinions were delivered in reverse order of seniority.

Analysis of Opinions.src: Congress proposed the \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution-conan/amendment-11/historical-background-on-eleventh-amendment}{Eleventh Amendment} on March 4, 1794, and States ratified it on February 7, 1795: ``The Judicial power of the United States shall not be construed to extend to any suit in law or equity, commenced or prosecuted against one of the United States by Citizens of another State, or by Citizens or Subjects of any Foreign State.''

Although the Court entered default judgment for Chisholm in 1794, no writ of inquiry was executed; in \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/3/378/}{\emph{Hollingsworth v. Virginia}, 3 U.S. (3 Dall.) 378 (1798)}, the Court unanimously dismissed all pending suits against States.

On March 4, 2026, in \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/607/24-1021/}{\emph{Galette v. New Jersey Transit Corp.}, 607 U.S. \_\_\_ (2026)}, a unanimous Court held that NJ Transit is a legally separate corporation responsible for its own judgments---not an ``arm of the State''---and therefore lacks interstate sovereign immunity.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (No Immunity Bar): The State as Plaintiff.} A Texas supplier sells generators to Louisiana and then refuses to honor its warranty. Flip the posture of a typical immunity case:

Examples: Future Applications.src: if \emph{Louisiana} sues the Texas supplier in federal court, immunity does not apply---creating the one-way asymmetry Chief Justice Jay criticized (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/2/419/}{2 U.S. at 473})

Examples: Future Applications.new: . The Eleventh Amendment reaches only suits ``commenced or prosecuted against'' a State, so Article III permits federal jurisdiction when the State sues. The Supreme Court has original, nonexclusive jurisdiction over such an action, and a lower federal court would need a separate statutory grant. Georgia likewise sued South Carolina citizens in the Supreme Court in \emph{Georgia v.\ Brailsford} while claiming immunity in \emph{Chisholm}.

\item \textbf{Same-Side (Relief Available): Prospective Relief Against a State Officer.} After Louisiana's legislature passes a statute cancelling its outstanding contracts with out-of-state suppliers, a Texas supplier sues the state treasurer in federal court, seeking an injunction against enforcement of the statute as a violation of the Contracts Clause. The suit may proceed: under \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/209/123/}{\emph{Ex parte Young}, 209 U.S.\ 123 (1908)}, a federal court may order a state officer to stop violating federal law prospectively, and the officer cannot shelter behind the State's immunity. This preserves part of the \emph{Chisholm} majority's concern that a State not escape its contracts without judicial accountability. The supplier cannot, however, obtain an order requiring payment of the past debt from the state treasury.
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Suit Barred): An Unpaid Contract Debt in Federal Court.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: A Texas supplier sues the State of Louisiana in federal court for \$15 million on an unpaid generator contract, alleging breach of contract and a Contracts Clause violation. Under \emph{Chisholm}, the suit proceeds (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/2/419/}{2 U.S. at 456}); today, it is barred by the \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution-conan/amendment-11/historical-background-on-eleventh-amendment}{Eleventh Amendment} and \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/134/1/}{\emph{Hans}}, and \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/209/123/}{\emph{Ex parte Young}} does not permit retroactive treasury damages.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Suit Barred): Federal Wage Claims in the State's Own Courts.} State probation officers in Maine sue the State in a Maine state court, seeking back overtime pay owed under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act. They argue that the Eleventh Amendment, which speaks only to ``the Judicial power of the United States,'' says nothing about state courts. Under \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/527/706/}{\emph{Alden v.\ Maine}, 527 U.S.\ 706 (1999)}, the suit is barred: Congress may not use its Article I powers to subject a nonconsenting State to private damages suits in its own courts. The result rests on the structural view of state sovereignty traced to Justice Iredell's dissent, not on the Amendment's text that the \emph{Chisholm} majority's textualism would have emphasized.

\item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Close Call): Is a State-Created Hospital Authority an ``Arm of the State''?} A State creates a public hospital authority as a separate corporation empowered to contract and to sue or be sued in its own name. Its charter makes it legally responsible for its own debts, but a later statute requires the State treasury to satisfy any final judgment against it above a specified threshold. An out-of-state vendor sues in federal court for unpaid invoices and seeks a judgment above that threshold. Under \textit{Galette v.\ New Jersey Transit Corp.}\ (2026), separate incorporation presumptively weighs against immunity, while a State's formal legal responsibility for judgments supports arm-of-the-State status. The question is whether the State's mandatory but limited assumption of liability, considered with the authority's independent legal status, rebuts that presumption.

Key Quotations.src: ``To the Constitution of the United States, the term SOVEREIGN, is totally unknown. There is but one place where it could have been used with propriety. But even in that place, it would not, perhaps, have comported with the delicacy of those who ordained and established that Constitution. They might have announced themselves `SOVEREIGN' people of the United States. But serenely conscious of the fact, they avoided the ostentatious declaration.''

``A state, like a merchant, makes a contract. A dishonest state, like a dishonest merchant, wilfully refuses to discharge it. The latter is amenable to a court of justice. Upon general principles of right, shall the former, when summoned to answer the fair demands of its creditor, be permitted, Proteus-like, to assume a new appearance, and to insult him and justice by declaring `I am a Sovereign state?' Surely not.''

``No such ideas obtain here; at the Revolution, the sovereignty devolved on the people, and they are truly the sovereigns of the country, but they are sovereigns without subjects (unless the African slaves among us may be so called), and have none to govern but themselves; the citizens of America are equal as fellow citizens, and as joint tenants in the sovereignty.''

``Every State in the Union, in every instance where its sovereignty has not been delegated to the United States, I consider to be as completely sovereign as the United States are in respect to the powers surrendered. The United States are sovereign as to all the powers of Government actually surrendered: each State in the Union is sovereign as to all the powers reserved.''
